opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the beginning it wasn't some grand, deliberate plan. Gezhi has a strong tradition in science competitions, so when you get there, the atmosphere kind of pulls you in. There were teachers who were very good at spotting students who enjoyed thinking about problems a bit more deeply than the regular curriculum required, and there were classmates who were already doing olympiad-style problems for fun. When you're fifteen or sixteen, that kind of environment matters a lot more than any abstract career consideration.

For me personally, I think the main reason was that I just liked the feeling of solving hard problems. Regular classes were fine, but competition problems felt different. They weren't about memorizing procedures. You'd stare at something for an hour, sometimes a whole afternoon, and then suddenly see the structure behind it. That moment was really addictive. Physics in particular appealed to me because it connected that problem-solving pleasure to something real: you write down a few principles, and somehow they describe how the world actually behaves.

There was also a practical side, of course. In China, doing well in competitions can open doors, for example a path to a top university that doesn't depend entirely on the gaokao. Everyone knew that, and I'd be lying if I said it didn't factor in. But I don't think that alone would have kept me going, because competition training is pretty intense and a lot of it is frankly grinding. If you don't genuinely enjoy it, it's hard to sustain.

Looking back, what I value most isn't the results. It's that competitions trained a certain habit: being comfortable sitting with a problem you don't know how to solve yet, and not panicking. That habit carried over into research later, whether in physics or in AI. Most of the time in research you're stuck, and the competition years were kind of my first real practice at being stuck productively.

r001.rationale: He says he enjoyed solving hard problems, but does not attribute his interest to trying things he was not yet good at.

r002.rationale: He describes Gezhi’s competition culture and teachers, but does not say he chose it over a more prestigious school to access a competition class.

r003.rationale: He mentions enjoying competitions and their practical benefits, but gives no perception that the competition class had little to lose or that this made him willing to take a chance.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it was a very deliberate choice at the beginning. When I got into Gezhi, I was just a kid from Shanghai who liked solving problems more than memorizing things. The school had a strong competition culture — there were teachers who'd been coaching physics and math olympiad for years, and seniors who had gotten into Tsinghua and Peking University through that route. So it was in the air. You walk in and the question isn't really "should I do competitions," it's "which one."

I ended up in physics because I liked that it was concrete. Math competitions can feel like a game with made-up rules, and I respect that, but physics felt like the rules were real — there's an actual world behind the problems. And I had a teacher who was very good at making you feel that. He'd give us a problem and instead of handing over the solution, he'd just ask, "what do you think is actually happening here?" That changed how I thought about learning.

The other honest reason is that the normal gaokao path felt like running a race where everyone is just trying to make fewer mistakes. Competitions were the opposite — you're rewarded for having one genuinely good idea. For a sixteen-year-old that's very attractive. You feel like your thinking matters, not just your discipline.

Looking back, it taught me two things that I still use every day. One is that being stuck for a long time is normal and not a sign that you're bad at something. In competition training you sit with a problem for hours, sometimes days. The second is that the best solutions are usually simple once you see them, and the whole skill is in the seeing. That's basically research. I didn't know that then, but the habits transferred almost directly.
